title: Taxes on assets: what future options would be restricted?

shots.narration: Proposition forty-two restricts certain future taxes. It focuses on owning personal property, including financial assets, and on taxes applied retroactively. Personal property here generally means assets other than real estate.
shots.headline: Personal property is more than household belongings
items: Financial assets and other personal property

shots.narration: California already taxes income from assets, such as investment gains, and some forms of personal property already have taxes. It generally does not tax simply owning stocks. The proposal is primarily about restricting new taxes, not issuing a refund.
shots.headline: Owning an asset versus earning income
items: Receive income or sell at a gain

shots.narration: Imagine a business owner reviewing the value of company assets.
shots.headline: What counts as ownership?

shots.narration: Owning equipment or shares is different from earning a profit. A rule against a new ownership tax does not, by itself, eliminate income taxes on profits or every tax the owner already pays.
shots.headline: Keep the tax bases separate
items: Existing taxes do not simply vanish

shots.narration: A budget analyst considers future options for raising revenue.
shots.headline: The proposal limits future choices

shots.narration: The measure would prohibit new state taxes on ownership of financial assets and other personal property. It also limits certain retroactive taxes: taxes applied to activities or periods before the tax was adopted.
shots.headline: Two restrictions

shots.narration: For illustration, a tax enacted later but applied to income earned in an earlier period is retroactive. The measure’s detailed rules determine what is prohibited; this is not a claim that every tax adjustment becomes impossible.
shots.headline: What does retroactive mean?

shots.narration: The analyst does not attach a specific dollar saving or loss. Future revenue might rise less because some tax options would be unavailable. The effect depends on what lawmakers or voters would otherwise propose.
shots.headline: No fixed fiscal amount

shots.narration: Prop forty-two could also prevent Prop forty’s wealth tax from taking effect if both pass and forty-two gets more yes votes. The conflict and its legal interpretation matter alongside the broader restrictions.
shots.headline: The connection to Prop 40

shots.narration: A voter might favor predictable rules for savings, investments, and business assets, or object to taxes that reach backward. They may also want to stop the proposed wealth tax. This is a choice about limiting government’s future taxing authority.
shots.headline: The case for YES

shots.narration: You might want future voters to retain more tax choices.
shots.headline: Your question: protection or lost flexibility?

shots.narration: Another voter could prefer deciding future tax proposals individually instead of restricting them in the constitution. They may want wealth-based revenue options during a funding shortfall, or support Prop forty. Keeping an option available does not mean every future tax must be adopted.
shots.headline: The case for NO

shots.narration: In the September PPIC survey of likely voters, 54 percent said yes, 43 percent no, and 4 percent were unsure. These are dated survey results, not votes already cast.
shots.headline: September snapshot: PPIC

shots.narration: A later September Berkeley survey found 43 percent yes, 34 percent no, and 23 percent undecided. Question wording and methods differ, so comparing polls does not by itself establish a trend.
shots.headline: September snapshot: Berkeley IGS
shots.poll_note: Berkeley IGS · Sept 15–20, 2026 · likely voters · about ±2 points

shots.narration: Yes imposes the new limits; no retains the state’s current options without itself creating a new tax. Visit our website for the fuller explanation, source links, and official voter guide. Compare the tradeoffs, then make your own informed choice.
shots.headline: Explore the full explanation
